passage: The panchayat had given the youth club one job, a Diwali cultural evening in the village school hall, and Lalit was in charge. He sat on the school steps with Afreen, who ran the dance group, and a calendar. "The evening is on the 1st. Everything else goes backward from that." He counted. "The hall needs booking with the headmaster three weeks before, so by the 10th. Invitation cards to the elders and the sarpanch two weeks before, the 17th. Rehearsals start on the 12th, every evening, full run on the 29th. The sweets order to Ramesh Kaka's shop by the 25th." Afreen watched him write each date in the margin. "You've given everything a deadline." "That's the point," Lalit said. "If the hall slips, nothing else has anywhere to go."

qa.q: When is the Diwali cultural evening?
Why did Lalit start from the date of the evening?
qa.a: He felt the pressure of being in charge and wanted each step to have a clear deadline so nothing would slip.

qa.q: What could Lalit add to make the plan safer?
qa.a: A spare day or two before the full run on the 29th, so a late booking or delay doesn't squeeze the final rehearsal.

qa.q: How might Afreen see Lalit's calendar?
qa.a: Afreen seems impressed that every step has a deadline, and can now plan the dance rehearsals around the dates.

grounding: Shows a student fixing the date of a Diwali cultural evening and counting back to set deadlines for the hall, invitations, rehearsals and food.

subtype: Approach: working backward from the date [Thinking]
passage: The school in Leicester held a Diwali cultural evening every November, and this year the student council had given it to Javier and Olga. Javier opened a spreadsheet and typed the date first: Friday 8 November, 6 pm. Then he worked backward, out loud. "Hall booking has to be confirmed with the office four weeks before, so by 11 October. Invitations to families go out three weeks before, 18 October. Performers need at least two weeks of rehearsals, so auditions by 21 October. Food from the parents' committee confirmed by 1 November." Olga, who had been planning to "sort it as we go", watched the column fill. "So if we miss the hall date, everything else shifts." "Exactly. The date doesn't move. We do." By the end of lunch every job had a deadline and a name next to it.

qa.q: Why did Javier type the date first?
qa.a: He felt calmer and more confident starting from the one fixed point, so every other step could be counted back from it.

qa.q: What else could Javier add to the spreadsheet?
qa.a: A few spare days before the event, so a late performer or food delay doesn't push the whole evening off track.

qa.q: How might Olga have felt watching the column fill?
qa.a: Olga probably felt surprised and relieved, seeing that sorting it as they went would not have worked.

grounding: Shows a student fixing the date of a Diwali evening and working backward to give the hall, invitations, rehearsals and food each a deadline.
